In 1905 the Bulgarian medical student Stamen Grigorov, working in Geneva, identified the bacterium that turns milk into yoghurt. It was later named Lactobacillus bulgaricus after his country.

Yoghurt had been eaten for thousands of years in the Balkans, Turkey, the Middle East and Central Asia, but almost unknown in western Europe. Grigorov studied yoghurt from his home in Bulgaria under the microscope and found the rod shaped bacterium that makes milk thick and sour.

His work caught the eye of Élie Metchnikoff at the Pasteur Institute in Paris, a Nobel winner who believed that the long lives of Bulgarian peasants came from their yoghurt. He promoted it as a health food, and a yoghurt fashion spread through Europe. In 1919 Isaac Carasso began selling yoghurt in Barcelona under the name Danone, the start of an industry. Bulgaria still treats yoghurt as part of its national identity, and its bacterium is in yoghurt worldwide.
sum: In 1905 the Bulgarian medical student Stamen Grigorov, working in Geneva, identified the bacterium that turns milk into yoghurt. It was later named Lactobacillus bulgaricus after his country.
